How this list is ordered

Four gates, in this order: does it run the set, can we prove how long, can it be bought today, then price. No score and no weighting.

The four gates in full

Applied in this order to every published US record. There is no score and no weighting — each gate either separates two machines or hands them to the next one.

  1. 1 Does it run the set?

    Every record is put through the compatibility engine against all of the loads at once — running watts against continuous output, the worst start-up instant against the surge ceiling, waveform where a load demands one. Green first, then the tight fits, then anything the engine could not read, then the machines that cannot do it. A machine that cannot start the load in front of it is not a cheaper option.

  2. 2 Can we prove how long?

    A runtime is only printed where the brand publishes what it takes to compute one — a usable-capacity coefficient, whether stated as depth of discharge and inverter efficiency or as one combined figure — and never from the number on the box. Records that reach the target sort first, records with a proven but shorter figure next (longest first: inside that band none of them does the job, so the one that gets closest wins), and records whose duration cannot be proven at all sort last inside their verdict band. That is a statement about published data, not about the hardware, and each of those rows says so.

  3. 3 Can it be bought today?

    A record under a verified out-of-stock policy, or one we may not sell into your state, sorts behind an equivalent one that can be bought. It stays on the list with the reason attached rather than disappearing. Whether WattPair happens to hold a purchase link for a record is not part of this gate and never moves it: a machine we cannot link to is ranked exactly as if we could, and simply carries no buy button.

  4. 4 Then price.

    Cheapest first, inside everything above. One mains standard and one currency per page, so every comparison is like for like. A record with no verified price sorts to the back of its own band — the absence of a price is not a low price.

The loads this ranks against

Why this set, and where its figures come from

A single 1/3–1/2 HP submersible sump pump, on its own. Storms bring other loads with them, but the pump is the one that decides whether the basement floods, and mixing in a fridge or a furnace blower would dilute the one number this page exists to get right: the pump’s own current, which two manufacturers of the same “1/3 HP” pump publish 87% apart from each other at full load. That gap is why this page ranks against the nameplate a reader’s own pump actually carries, not a horsepower rating.

Why 12 hours

Twelve hours, to match the site’s home-backup default — but this is the one scenario on the site where the target duration cannot change the outcome. We have found no published figure for how many times a sump pump cycles per hour, because that number depends on how fast groundwater is entering a specific basement, not on the pump — so no station on this page can be shown to last any number of hours on this load, at 4 h or at 48 h alike. What changes with the target is nothing; what this page can prove is whether the pump starts at all.

Sump pump: we have found no published figure for how much of the time that load actually runs, and this library will not assume one. No energy target is stated for the set, and no runtime is computed from one. The verdicts are unaffected — they never read a duty cycle.

Why 7 records carry no printable runtime

7 of the 12 records here start and hold this load set and still carry no runtime this page will print — not because of anything a brand did, but because we have found no duty cycle and no modulation curve published for Sump pump. There is therefore no average draw to divide any battery by, for any station here, however completely that station documents its own coefficients. Why we could not find that figure for this particular load is set out above, under the duration target. That holds regardless of disclosure quality, and this page can put a number on it: 7 of the 12 records here do publish the depth of discharge and the inverter efficiency an hour figure is computed from — the same 7 that carry proven runtimes on this site's other lists — and on this load they print nothing either. The gate sits on the load, not on anyone’s battery documentation.

This page cannot even offer the fallback bound the other pages on this site print. That bound is a nameplate divided by the set’s own average draw, and the average draw is exactly what is missing — with no duty cycle to weight it by, there is nothing to divide any capacity above by, for any row here, cheap or expensive. Every capacity in the ranked list above is still each manufacturer’s own published figure; it is the arithmetic connecting it to a number of hours that cannot be done for this load.

The scope of that finding, stated: as of 2026-08-08 the manufacturer documents behind this load were read in full for a duty cycle or a modulation curve, and none exists in them. That is a statement about this ONE load record, not about the 7 stations paired with it here — each of those is judged on its own disclosure everywhere else on this site, and none of them is being marked down for it. This is a statement about published data, not about the hardware — the verdict column judges that separately, and it comes first.

The load that changes the answer

Add a well pump to the same set and the first gate, which was already turning records away, tightens further: not one of the 12 clears it outright — 1 is a tight fit and 11 cannot do it at all. The reason is one instant: a well pump asks for 6,762 W at start-up on its own, against 2,645 W for everything on the list above put together. That start-up figure is a published locked-rotor rating for an induction motor of this size. A sump pump’s own measured locked-rotor current is unusually low for a motor its size — well under the NEC table a lot of sizing advice still quotes. A well pump is not the same machine wearing a different label, and this is why you check the nameplate rather than the horsepower. The quiz carries this set as a preset.

Questions people ask about this list

How many of the 12 actually run it?
7 of 12 do, and the other 5 are the finding on this page. 720 W of running draw and 2,645 W at the worst start-up instant is what every published US record is measured against, and 5 of 12 are refused outright — on continuous output, surge ceiling and VA ceiling. Which means the buying question splits in two: whether a given machine starts it at all, and only then how long it holds. The ranked list above answers them in that order.
Is my pump the pump this list was ranked against?
Check the amps on it, not the horsepower. The 920 above is a Liberty 280-series 1/2 hp at its published full-load current — 8.0 A at 115 V — and this record’s own band runs 598 to 1,116 on the same basis: a Liberty 250-series 1/3 hp at 5.2 A at the bottom, a shaded-pole Zoeller M53 of the same nominal class at 9.7 A at the top, with no average of the two describing a real pump. One thing about all three figures: they are strictly volt-amps rather than watts. We have found no power factor published for these motors by either maker, so amps times volts is everything the record can hold — and volt-amps is what an inverter has to supply in any case, which is why the check made above is still the right one.
Why is the start-up figure so much lower than the sizing tables say?
Because of the motor, and because the table is not a measurement. Liberty prints full-load and locked-rotor amps on the same line of the same sheet: 8.0 A and 23 A on the 1/2 hp, a ratio of 2.88, and 5.2 A and 8 A on the 1/3 hp, a ratio of 1.54. NEC Table 430.251(A) puts a 1/2 HP 115 V motor at 58.8 A instead — a flat six times its own full-load table — but that table’s header limits it to sizing breakers, controllers and disconnects. It is a selection envelope, not something measured on a pump. The motors in these pumps are shaded-pole and permanent-split-capacitor; neither is a capacitor-start design, and neither draws a capacitor-start inrush. A 1/2 HP well pump, by contrast, really does draw 58.8 A at start on its own maker’s published figure — same horsepower, different machine, and the envelope fits that one. Size a sump pump against the envelope and you refuse stations that start it.
